cells.tense: You are here with the pen, choosing which pull to follow and letting what you tend set part of its pace.
cells.act: give a concrete piece of help and finish it
cells.ask: Think of what you're helping along. Give it a piece of help with a clear end, and when that's reached, stop. The finishing is the offer.
cells.core:
What you're tending is close enough now that you can see its shape and still hear what it's reaching toward, without one crowding the other. That's what lets help land instead of hover. When this is working, you hand something over and step back, and the growing thing keeps going on the strength that was already in it.

So give one finishable piece of help. Something with a clear end, so whoever or whatever you're tending can carry it from there. Finishing is the point. The help goes over; what stays with you is the ability to see clearly enough to step back once it's given.
cells.sheetLine: Give one useful thing, finish it, and step back.
cells.verb: choosing which pull to follow next
cells.place: the quiet shelf where something newly grown is still being tended

cells.tense: You are steering ahead of what you're tending, planning for a harvest that isn't ready to be named yet.
cells.act: let several things be true and act on one
cells.ask: When you catch yourself mapping a future for someone you care about, name three things that could be true, then act only on the one that fits what's happening now.
cells.core:
You can hold the many shapes a thing might take — that's a real gift. The trouble is doing it at a distance, planning for a child or a project as though the harvest were already visible. Likely you can see four or five things it might become, and you're trying to feed all of them at once. What gets lost is the thing's own timing.

Let several futures stand and pick one. Not the best one — the one that fits what's actually here today. Then act on it, and only on it. The pull to plan ahead is strong. Spent on one real thing instead of the whole forecast, your attention settles where the growing is happening now.
cells.sheetLine: Pick one of the futures and act on today's.

cells.tense: You stood at a door that's already behind you, and part of you is still waiting there while time moves on.
cells.act: take pleasure in the grown thing
cells.ask: Sit with something you grew and haven't enjoyed — a habit, a room, a friendship. No improving. Enjoyment is the whole job those minutes.
cells.core:
A harvest you raised has come in, and you're still out in the field checking on rows, as if stopping to eat were a way of losing the plot. What's here is real and finished enough. What's missing is the part where it's yours to enjoy. The field is done.

Sit with the result for a few minutes instead of facing the next task. Time with something you actually made happen and haven't properly taken in. Not upkeep — enjoyment is what those minutes are for. Care in you doesn't run down by resting; it comes back charged. What's grown is allowed to be eaten.
cells.sheetLine: The field is grown. Eat something from it.

cells.tense: You are holding a shape steady for something that is growing, and it would surprise you to hear it called care.
cells.act: share your strength where it is needed
cells.ask: The next concrete help someone near you needs, do it yourself and say out loud that it's yours. Not anonymous, not disguised. Let them hear who did it.
cells.core:
You are the steady one near something that's growing — you keep the hard hours off it and keep it fed while it takes its shape. Done quietly, often while calling it something else. The person or thing being held doesn't think of it as care, because nobody names it that way.

Share your strength where it's actually needed, and say whose it is. One piece of concrete help, delivered aloud. Saying it says what quiet holding doesn't: this is mine to give, and you're why. Care doesn't get better by being renamed. It gets better by being noticed — including by you.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding it steady. Say so out loud.

attempts.check: The weakest claim is that the person is 'steering without noticing' in the Unacknowledged cell — the record names the misattribution but not the person's own account of it, and a reader could fairly say they are simply deciding fast because others depend on them. The Too Much cell presumes the person's care is running ahead of a child's or a project's pace; a reader could say the pace is the other person's and the bracing is reasonable. The ask in each cell stands alone if the read is wrong: it is one small act from the medicine, not a diagnosis, and doing it teaches something either way. The sentence that serves me is 'the weight stays held while a form never gets to take its own shape' — it is a line I would enjoy writing more than the person needs to hear; I am cutting it back to a plain statement of what the mechanism does.
